payload.title: What Are the Wedding Traditions Worth Keeping?
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s, affluent, interested in a destination wedding and other luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: A couple in their mid 30s (typically Sydney or Melbourne, AUD 150k to 300k budget, 60 to 90 guests, many flying in) about a year out, who want a ceremony that feels personal rather than inherited by default, and are deciding which traditions to keep, adapt or quietly drop, including which local customs they could borrow at their destination without it feeling like a costume.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor about building a ceremony that blends family traditions with local customs at the destination.
payload.service_link: /magazine (primary, UTM-tagged); /wonderland-concierge (secondary, UTM-tagged, placed in the destination traditions section where the question 'how do we include this legally and respectfully abroad?' is raised)
payload.angle: Most page-one results are listicles of 'fun facts' that repeat contested origin myths (the vein of love, bridesmaids as decoys, 'honeymoon' from a month of mead) as if they were history. We give the documented origin of each tradition, flag clearly where the popular story is folklore, and then make an honest editorial call on whether it is worth keeping, adapting or skipping today, with the practical view of a destination wedding planner: what travels well, what clashes with local law or venue rules, and which local customs at popular destinations couples can borrow respectfully.

traditions_to_cover.tradition: Engagement and wedding rings on the fourth finger of the left hand
facts_to_source: Roman use of betrothal rings (museum collection object records, e.g. British Museum Roman betrothal / fede rings)

Where the 'vena amoris' (vein to the heart) idea is first recorded in English (often attributed to Henry Swinburne's treatise on spousals, late 1600s) and that it is anatomically untrue: write as 'often said'
Ring exchange in the marriage service (e.g. Book of Common Prayer 1549 text, from the Church of England or British Library)
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: keep; note variations (right hand in several European and Orthodox traditions) [[VERIFY: which countries, from a reputable source]]

facts_to_source: Roman flammeum (flame-coloured veil) worn by brides (encyclopaedia or museum source)
Any documented religious meaning in Jewish (bedeken) or Christian ceremony
Avoid the 'hide the bride from evil spirits' line unless a reputable source documents it; otherwise 'often said'
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: keep or adapt; modern options (no veil, cathedral veil for church settings, short veil for beach heat)

facts_to_source: Queen Victoria's white satin wedding dress, 10 February 1840, and its role in popularising white (Royal Collection Trust or V&A)
That brides before then often wore their best dress in any colour (V&A or museum costume collection)
Red as the traditional bridal colour in China and India (encyclopaedia or museum source)
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: adapt freely; colour and outfit changes are common at multi-day destination weddings

traditions_to_cover.tradition: Something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue (and a sixpence)
facts_to_source: Earliest documented printed version of the rhyme (Victorian England, 19th century; folklore dictionary, national library or OED-type source)
The sixpence line: its documented origin and that the coin is no longer minted (Royal Mint or British Museum)
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: keep; easy, personal, travels well; suggest family heirlooms as 'something borrowed'

traditions_to_cover.tradition: Bridesmaids, groomsmen and the wedding party
facts_to_source: Roman requirement for witnesses at a marriage (encyclopaedia source)
The 'bridesmaids dressed alike to confuse evil spirits' story: only include as 'often said' if a reputable source discusses it as folklore; otherwise leave out
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: adapt; mixed-gender parties, 'people of honour', smaller parties to reduce guests' travel cost

traditions_to_cover.tradition: Giving away and walking down the aisle
facts_to_source: Wording of 'Who giveth this woman' in the Book of Common Prayer and its optional status in current Church of England services
Legal history only if a reputable source documents it (avoid unsourced 'property transfer' claims)
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: adapt; both parents, walking together, walking alone; describe accurately and never mock

facts_to_source: Origin of the familiar English vow wording ('to have and to hold', 'till death us do part') in the Book of Common Prayer (1549/1662)

Australian requirement for the legal vow wording (Attorney-General's Department guidance for marriage celebrants) [[VERIFY: current wording requirement and whether it applies to a marriage held overseas]]
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: keep; link to vows pages rather than repeating them

facts_to_source: Meaning of handfasting as a form of betrothal or marriage in medieval and early modern Scotland and England (National Records of Scotland, National Museums Scotland, or encyclopaedia)
That the modern symbolic cord ceremony is largely a 20th-century revival (reputable heritage or academic source); contested 'year and a day' claims written as 'often said'
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: keep as symbolic; popular in symbolic ceremonies abroad where the legal marriage happens at home

facts_to_source: Its place in African American history, especially among enslaved couples denied legal marriage (Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture or Library of Congress)
Documented British (Welsh, Romani) broomstick marriage references, written carefully and only if sourced
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: keep where it is part of the couple's heritage; explain respectfully, not as a novelty

facts_to_source: Talmudic source usually cited (Berakhot 30b to 31a) and the common interpretation linking it to remembering the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem (Jewish encyclopaedia, Jewish museum or Britannica)
Note that interpretations vary; present more than one, sourced
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: keep where part of the couple's faith or heritage; venue logistics (glass wrapped in cloth, cleaning up)

traditions_to_cover.tradition: Wedding cake and cutting the cake
facts_to_source: Roman confarreatio and the cake of spelt (farreum) (encyclopaedia source)

Queen Victoria's 1840 wedding cake (Royal Collection Trust) and how tiered white cakes became the norm (museum or library source) [[VERIFY: tiered cake attribution, often linked to the 1858 royal wedding or later]]
Croquembouche in France and other national cakes only if sourced
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: adapt; local desserts at the destination (e.g. Italian millefoglie) as an alternative [[VERIFY: local dessert examples]]

traditions_to_cover.tradition: The bouquet and the bouquet toss
facts_to_source: Use of herbs and flowers by brides in classical and medieval weddings (encyclopaedia or museum)
Victorian floriography and orange blossom (Queen Victoria wore orange blossom, Royal Collection Trust)
Bouquet toss origin is myth-prone: write as 'often said' or leave the origin out
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: adapt or skip; toss is falling out of favour; alternatives (anniversary dance, giving it to a grandparent)

facts_to_source: Grain thrown as a fertility symbol in ancient and later European weddings (encyclopaedia source)
Etymology of 'confetti' from Italian sugared almonds (Treccani or OED-type dictionary)
Note that many venues and some destinations restrict confetti or rice: [[VERIFY: do not name specific bans without a source]]
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: adapt; biodegradable petals or dried flowers, check venue rules

facts_to_source: Roman custom of lifting the bride over the threshold and Plutarch's discussion of it in Roman Questions (Perseus Digital Library, LacusCurtius or Loeb edition)
Why it was done is contested even in Plutarch: present his suggested reasons as his, not as fact
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: skip or keep for fun; at a destination it becomes the villa or suite door

facts_to_source: Earliest recorded use of the word 'honeymoon' in English, 16th century, and its original meaning (OED or Merriam-Webster)
The 'month of mead' story is folklore: label it 'often said' or leave it out
Wedding trips becoming common in the 19th century (encyclopaedia or library source)
traditions_to_cover.editorial_call: keep; link honeymoon guides; at a destination wedding the honeymoon often follows on from the same trip

destination_section.heading_suggestion: Local wedding traditions you can borrow at your destination
destination_section.brief: Short entries (60 to 120 words each) for popular destinations. Each: what the custom is, a sourced line on its meaning, how guests or couples can take part respectfully, and a link to our deeper page where one exists. Do not repeat content from those pages; summarise and link.

entries.customs_to_consider: confetti (sugared almonds) and bomboniere, la serenata, toasting 'evviva gli sposi'
entries.facts_to_source: Sulmona confetti tradition; odd-number almond custom only if sourced

entries.destination: Lebanon and the Levant (and Lebanese weddings held abroad)
entries.customs_to_consider: the zaffe procession with drums and dancers
entries.facts_to_source: what a zaffe is, from an encyclopaedia, museum or cultural heritage source

entries.customs_to_consider: henna night, separate or mixed celebrations, Arabic coffee and hospitality customs
entries.facts_to_source: henna in wedding custom (UNESCO intangible heritage listing for henna, if applicable) [[VERIFY]]
definitions from an encyclopaedia (Britannica, Oxford Islamic Studies) only

entries.customs_to_consider: mehndi, haldi, the saat phere around the sacred fire, the baraat
entries.facts_to_source: saat phere and agni from an encyclopaedia or museum source; fire rules at venues are a [[VERIFY]] per venue

entries.customs_to_consider: stefana (crowns) in the Greek Orthodox ceremony, koufeta (sugared almonds)
entries.link: none on site (link map); no internal link
entries.facts_to_source: stefana in the Orthodox rite from an Orthodox church or encyclopaedia source

entries.customs_to_consider: el lazo (the cord or rosary around the couple), las arras (13 coins)
entries.facts_to_source: lazo and arras from an encyclopaedia, museum or national cultural source

entries.customs_to_consider: san-san-kudo, the shared sake ritual in a Shinto ceremony
entries.facts_to_source: san-san-kudo from a Japanese cultural or shrine source, or encyclopaedia
quaich from National Museums Scotland or similar

destination_section.respect_note: Borrowed customs should be framed as 'invite a local to lead it' or 'ask your celebrant or venue', not as decoration. Religious rites (stefana, nikah, saat phere) are described as part of their faith, not offered as props for couples outside it.

internal_links.where: close or FAQ (traditions for anniversaries / renewals), optional
Secondary CTA in destination section and close

must_include: For each tradition: what it is, where it comes from (sourced, with contested origins labelled 'often said' plus the documented version, or omitted), and our clearly framed editorial call: keep, adapt or skip, with a destination-wedding angle
A myth-versus-documented-history thread: at least 3 traditions where we correct a popular origin story using a reputable source (ring vein, honeymoon mead, bridesmaid decoys or bouquet toss)
Destination section on local traditions to borrow, linking our existing Italy, Indian, Muslim, Arab and Lebanese pages and the vows pages rather than repeating them
Inclusive, gender-neutral modern adaptations wherever the tradition allows; traditions that assume a bride and groom described accurately, never mocked

One practical destination-wedding point per relevant tradition (for example venue rules on confetti, open flame or glass; legal versus symbolic ceremony for handfasting and vows) with anything factual sourced or marked [[VERIFY]]
A short 'how to decide which traditions to keep' framework (meaning to you, meaning to family, practicality abroad)

FAQ of 3 to 6 questions from the SEO researcher's PAA set (e.g. 'What are the oldest wedding traditions?', 'Do you have to follow wedding traditions?', 'What is the something old, something new tradition?')
avoid: Copying or paraphrasing the old page's copy (it is not recoverable anyway) or any competitor copy, especially Easy Weddings
Stating any origin story as fact without a reputable source (encyclopaedia, museum, national library, academic or heritage body); no invented etymology
Prices of any kind (person's standard), and any Advisor or business claim not in brand-facts.md
Vendor names unless linked to their profile in context
Mocking or exoticising any culture or faith; presenting religious rites as décor for couples outside that faith
Garter removal and toss as a featured tradition (low fit for this audience; at most a one-line mention in the bouquet section if the SEO data shows demand)
Superstition stacking ('bad luck to see the bride') without source; if included, label as superstition
Em dashes, American spelling, stacked superlatives
Legal claims about marrying abroad (recognition in Australia, celebrant wording) without [[VERIFY]] or an official source

payload.regional_scope_note: First pass: global. The topic is cultural, not market-specific; AU-specific points (legal vow wording, recognition of overseas marriage) handled as sourced asides. SEO researcher may recommend otherwise from the 5-city SERP check.

'Wedding Traditions', 'Ceremony', 'Cultural Weddings' and 'Destination Weddings' exist or can be created as site categories (link map topics show 'ceremony' and 'cultural weddings'; others inferred).
Content type mapped to planning_guide because the schema has no 'pillar' value.

Old page content is unknown, so 'keep the ones the old page covers' cannot be applied directly; the 15 traditions are the commonly searched 'oldest' traditions, to be checked against ranked queries by the SEO researcher.

Australian legal vow wording requirement and whether it applies to a marriage held overseas (Attorney-General's Department)

Tiered white wedding cake attribution (1840 vs 1858 royal weddings or later)
Local dessert alternatives named at destinations
Any destination or venue confetti/rice restrictions
